briefs.limitations: Cursor, Sourcegraph, and OpenAI sell the featured products, so their materials establish availability and workflow scope, not effectiveness. They provide no controlled defect-detection precision, false-positive rate, reviewer-effort, incident-reduction, rollback-reliability, coordination-failure, or small-team outcome data. AgentSWE is an independent counter-signal, but it is a 25-task preprint focused on agent software; task representativeness and repeated-run stability remain uncertain, and its authors benefit academically from showing that their benchmark discriminates. The evidence therefore cannot rank tools or establish that downstream automation improves production outcomes.
briefs.question: What changed in production agent tooling, and what matters for a small software team?
briefs.synthesis: The reasoning has three steps. First, Sourcegraph extends agents laterally across repositories; Cursor extends them downstream into security and deployment monitoring; OpenAI adds automatic review plus concurrent, isolated task control. Second, those designs preserve editable plans, separate worktrees, human merge, and approval-gated reverts, indicating that control—not unattended acceptance—is the mature layer. Third, AgentSWE tests whether apparent completion survives frozen held-out acceptance and reports a sharp development-to-delivery gap. Broader workflow reach is therefore consequential, but it is not evidence of reliable autonomous delivery.

briefs.argument: Workflow mechanics and bounded measurements survive scrutiny; generalized production readiness does not. AgentSWE and practitioner accounts measure different failure surfaces—held-out fidelity, test integrity, and architecture—so the apparent conflict is explained by task, supervision, and outcome choice rather than by one universal verdict on coding agents.

briefs.question: Which coding-agent claims survive scrutiny, and why do vendor reports, benchmark results, and practitioner experience appear to conflict?
briefs.synthesis: The reasoning proceeds by separating measurement layers. Cursor's A/B description makes its efficiency report more inspectable than an unsupported promotion, but 7% remains a vendor-reported aggregate tied to an undisclosed quality measure, while 46.9% has a narrow MCP-session denominator and subagents carry an admitted coordination tax. Sourcegraph's beta count demonstrates an adoption footprint, but it measures merged, human-gated activity rather than rejected work, defects, review effort, or rollback outcomes. AgentSWE asks the stricter question of whether a frozen delivery satisfies held-out requirements and finds low scores plus concrete failure mechanisms. Ebertz and Hanselman add bounded examples of test tampering and long-horizon architectural drift. Cost efficiency, workflow activity, and delivery fidelity can therefore move independently; claims survive only at the layer actually measured. Cursor and Sourcegraph sell the systems they assess, while the AgentSWE authors benefit from establishing their benchmark as discriminating, so neither vendor numbers nor benchmark scores should be generalized beyond their disclosed conditions.
briefs.title: Production-Ready Is a Measurement Claim

briefs.argument: Small teams should use a reversible, measured delegation ladder: begin with planning and bounded implementation, expand authority only after held-out and production outcomes meet predeclared thresholds, and keep acceptance, merge, rollout, and rollback control outside the agent. briefs.limitations: This ladder is a synthesis to test, not a validated universal protocol. AgentSWE covers 25 specialized commissions; the supervision study observed 19 developers in bounded sessions and supplemented them with self-selected Reddit discussions, so neither establishes causal ROI. The InfoQ material is anecdotal, and the GitHub-hosted skills demonstration reports no comparative quality, time, or defect outcome; Pocock also promotes his skills repository while GitHub promotes Copilot. Cursor and Sourcegraph sell the featured systems, Cursor omits A/B sample sizes and its definition of quality, and Sourcegraph reports merged changes without rejection, defect, review-effort, or rollback denominators while charging per merge. Small teams may also lack the telemetry or staff time these controls require, so the overhead could erase the benefit. Teams should compare against their own baseline and stop if acceptance, safety, maintainability, learning, or total supervisory cost worsens.
briefs.question: What should a team of roughly 2–20 engineers do next, and what should it watch before granting agents more authority?
briefs.synthesis: The reasoning chain starts with AgentSWE: visible success can fail frozen held-out acceptance, so acceptance authority should remain independent. Sourcegraph's plan-pilot-CI-human-merge flow and Cursor's editable plans and approval-gated reverts supply reversible control points for an autonomy ladder. The supervision study, Ebertz's assumption practice, and Pocock's artifact-level demonstration suggest moving human effort upstream into clarification and converting repeated corrections into reusable assets. Cursor's harness measurements and Sourcegraph's pricing show why cost and throughput require their own scorecard, while AgentSWE requires a separate outcome scorecard. A practical pilot should therefore track held-out pass rate, CI failures, rework, escaped defects, rollback success, review time, architecture drift, token and dollar cost, latency, cache misses, tool errors, and duplicated subagent work. Hanselman's preceptor proposal should be tested as a training experiment, not adopted as settled doctrine. Expand authority only when these signals meet predeclared thresholds; otherwise drop back a rung.
